title: Sanitizers, static analysis and memory-checking workflow (CodeSaathi extension)
learningObjectives: Explain the topic and its C rules.
Trace the example and explain its data or control flow.
Identify edge cases and resource-management requirements.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: A defensive C workflow combines compiler warnings, static analysis, runtime sanitizers, targeted tests and review of ownership and bounds. Static analysis inspects code without executing every path; sanitizers instrument executed paths to detect selected runtime defects.
understand.whyItMatters: No single tool proves a C program safe. Layered checks provide independent evidence and make defects easier to reproduce and diagnose.
understand.analogy: Treat each algorithm or resource as a contract whose invariants must remain true after every operation.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal rules for pointers, object lifetime, complexity or library contracts.

explain.narrative:
A defensive C workflow combines compiler warnings, static analysis, runtime sanitizers, targeted tests and review of ownership and bounds. Static analysis inspects code without executing every path; sanitizers instrument executed paths to detect selected runtime defects.

State preconditions, invariants, empty and full cases, ownership and failure behaviour before implementation. Compile with warnings and test normal, boundary and failure paths.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The build requests warnings and runtime instrumentation on a supported toolchain. The test suite must exercise relevant paths for runtime tools to observe them.

practise.guidedTask: List which defects static analysis may find and which require executing a test path.
practise.independentTask: Create a repeatable debug build and test checklist. Record tool versions and unresolved findings.
hints: Run the same deterministic tests in ordinary and diagnostic builds.
A clean sanitizer run does not prove that unexecuted paths are correct.
Treat each diagnostic as evidence to investigate, not as a substitute for understanding.

questions.prompt: What should be verified before relying on the implementation?
options: Preconditions, invariants, bounds and failure cases.
Only the name of the algorithm.
Whether one input produced a result.
questions.answer: Preconditions, invariants, bounds and failure cases.
questions.explanation: Correctness depends on maintaining the data structure or algorithm contract.

questions.prompt: Which test strategy is most useful?
options: Test empty, boundary and representative operation sequences.
Assume one successful example proves all cases.
questions.answer: Test empty, boundary and representative operation sequences.
questions.explanation: Targeted tests expose defects ordinary examples can miss.
